extracted.intended_audience: conference reviewers, area chairs, and program chairs (NeurIPS/ML peer-review participants)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and metrics for reviewers, area chairs, and program chairs on scoring, commenting, and calibrating peer review for NeurIPS (2014), plus system-level metrics used to evaluate consistency of committee decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Numerical quality score (1–10) and interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers give a score of between 1 and 10 for each paper. The program committee will interpret the numerical score in the following way: 10: Top 5% of accepted NIPS papers, a seminal paper for the ages. I will consider not reviewing for NIPS again if this is rejected. 9: Top 15% of accepted NIPS papers, an excellent paper, a strong accept. I will fight for acceptance. 8: Top 50% of accepted NIPS papers, a very good paper, a clear accept. I vote and argue for acceptance. 7: Good paper, accept. I vote for acceptance, although would not be upset if it were rejected. 6: Marginally above the acceptance threshold. I tend to vote for accepting it, but leaving it out of the program would be no great loss. 5: Marginally below the acceptance threshold. I tend to vote for rejecting it, but having it in the program would not be that bad. 4: An OK paper, but not good enough. A rejection. I vote for rejecting it, although would not be upset if it were accepted. 3: A clear rejection. I vote and argue for rejection. 2: A strong rejection. I’m surprised it was submitted to this conference. I will fight for rejection. 1: Trivial or wrong or known. I’m surprised anybody wrote such a paper. I will consider not reviewing for NIPS again if this is accepted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scores should reflect absolute judgments of the contributions made by each paper. Reviewers should NOT assume they have received an unbiased sample of papers, nor should they adjust their scores to achieve an artificial balance of high and low scores. (Recommendation noted elsewhere that '6' is a recommended accept threshold.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact score (binary: 1 or 2)
rubrics_metrics.description: Independently of the Quality Score, this is your opportunity to identify papers that are very different, original, or otherwise potentially impactful for the NIPS community. There are two choices: 2: This work is different enough from typical submissions to potentially have a major impact on a subset of the NIPS community. 1: This work is incremental and unlikely to have much impact even though it may be technically correct and well executed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the impact score to flag papers that, even if technically imperfect, could stimulate new directions. Be aware examples exist where impact and quality disagree (technically strong but unlikely to generate follow-up, or technically flawed but potentially direction-setting).

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidence score (1–5) and interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers also give a confidence score between 1 and 5 for each paper. The program committee will interpret the numerical score in the following way: 5: The reviewer is absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct and very familiar with the relevant literature. 4: The reviewer is confident but not absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct. It is unlikely but conceivable that the reviewer did not understand certain parts of the paper, or that the reviewer was unfamiliar with a piece of relevant literature. 3: The reviewer is fairly confident that the evaluation is correct. It is possible that the reviewer did not understand certain parts of the paper, or that the reviewer was unfamiliar with a piece of relevant literature. Mathematics and other details were not carefully checked. 2: The reviewer is willing to defend the evaluation, but it is quite likely that the reviewer did not understand central parts of the paper. 1: The reviewer’s evaluation is an educated guess. Either the paper is not in the reviewer’s area, or it was extremely difficult to understand.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report confidence honestly to help area chairs weigh reviews; confidence correlates with citation outcomes in retrospective analysis, so it is a meaningful meta-indicator.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualitative evaluation: Quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the paper technically sound? Are claims well-supported by theoretical analysis or experimental results? Is this a complete piece of work, or merely a position paper? Are the authors careful (and honest) about evaluating both the strengths and weaknesses of the work?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comment on technical soundness, evidence supporting claims, completeness of the contribution, and whether weaknesses are acknowledged and tested.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualitative evaluation: Clarity
rubrics_metrics.description: Is the paper clearly written? Is it well-organized? (If not, feel free to make suggestions to improve the manuscript.) Does it adequately inform the reader? (A superbly written paper provides enough information for the expert reader to reproduce its results.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess organization, readability, and reproducibility of results; provide concrete suggestions to improve exposition where needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualitative evaluation: Originality
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the problems or approaches new? Is this a novel combination of familiar techniques? Is it clear how this work differs from previous contributions? Is related work adequately referenced?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recommend checking recent NIPS proceedings to ensure novelty; explicitly state how the paper differs from prior work and whether references are sufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualitative evaluation: Significance
rubrics_metrics.description: Are the results important? Are other people (practitioners or researchers) likely to use these ideas or build on them? Does the paper address a difficult problem in a better way than previous research? Does it advance the state of the art in a demonstrable way? Does it provide unique data, unique conclusions on existing data, or a unique theoretical or pragmatic approach?
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge potential uptake and advancement of the field; indicate whether contribution moves state-of-the-art or provides unique resources/insights.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instruction: Reviewers should comment on all four qualitative criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: All NIPS papers should be good scientific papers, regardless of their specific area. We judge whether a paper is good using four criteria; a reviewer should comment on all of these, if possible: Quality, Clarity, Originality, Significance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, explicitly provide comments addressing each of the four criteria to aid area chairs and authors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer load and assignment guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: To keep quality of reviews high, we tried to keep load low. We didn’t assign any reviewer more than 5 papers, most reviewers received 4 papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limit per-reviewer assignments to reduce fatigue and maintain review quality; recruit area chairs early and use prior publication records to select reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Don’t adjust scores for sample bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers should NOT assume that they have received an unbiased sample of papers, nor should they adjust their scores to achieve an artificial balance of high and low scores. Scores should reflect absolute judgments of the contributions made by each paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid normalization or rank-rescaling within your assigned set; provide absolute assessments per the score definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recommendation threshold guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Quality of papers is scored on a 10-point scale with a recommendation of 6 being accept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat '6' as the marginally above-threshold accept recommendation when mapping quality score to acceptance tendency; combine with impact/confidence and AC judgment.

rubrics_metrics.name: System-level consistency metrics (inconsistency, accept precision, reject precision, agreed accept rate)
rubrics_metrics.description: Metrics used to summarize agreement between independent committees: inconsistency = proportion of decisions that were not the same across two committees. Accept precision = probability any accepted paper would be rejected in a rerunning (operationalized via committee-specific fractions). Reject precision = probability any rejected paper would be rejected in a rerunning. Agreed accept rate = ratio of consistent accepts to consistent rejects (or the fraction of papers agreed accepted).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use confusion-matrix style counts across duplicated reviews to compute these statistics; present with uncertainty (e.g., binomial/Dirichlet or Monte Carlo) to account for sampling variability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental protocol for measuring consistency: duplicated reviews (~10%)
rubrics_metrics.description: To explore consistency, select approximately 10% of submitted papers to be reviewed twice by independent committees (170 papers in 2014). Divide the program committee into two independent committees and randomly place reviewers on one side or the other; ensure program chair selections provide expert coverage across areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When running a duplication experiment, randomize reviewer placement, ensure AC coverage, and treat duplicated papers identically to others in assignment and process; be aware ACs in 2014 knew which papers were duplicates (possible bias).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer calibration model (score decomposition and offset estimation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Model assumption: the score from the jth reviewer for the ith paper is y_{i,j} = f_i + b_j + epsilon_{i,j} where f_i is the 'objective quality' of paper i, b_j is an offset associated with reviewer j, and epsilon is subjective noise. With normal priors on f and b and noise variance sigma^2, one can estimate reviewer offsets (calibration) and underlying paper quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use calibration to adjust for reviewer bias when possible; note data requirements (many reviewers with few papers each limit per-reviewer parameter estimation) and that simplifying distributional assumptions reduce parameters to a manageable set (e.g., m + 3). Calibration methods (e.g., Bayesian) can produce adjusted, comparable quality estimates across reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review timeliness, length, and confidence as indicators of review quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Empirical findings: late reviews (after the reviewing deadline) were on average less confident and shorter, but rate papers as higher quality (small effects ~5%). Statistical tests showed small but significant differences: confidence (p ≈ 0.048), quality score (p ≈ 0.007), review length difference (~100 words, p ≈ 0.55%).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monitor submission timing and consider that late reviews may differ systematically: shorter, lower confidence, but slightly more generous in quality/impact ratings. Use timeliness as one factor when weighting or interrogating review reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Bayesian/uncertainty quantification for system metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: When estimating probabilities such as consistent accept/inconsistent/consistent reject, model counts with a multinomial likelihood and use a Dirichlet prior (e.g., uniform Dir(1,1,1)) to compute posterior means and variances; use Monte Carlo sampling from the posterior to compute derived statistics (accept precision, reject precision, agreed accept rate) and their uncertainties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report error bars (e.g., +/- two standard deviations or percentiles) for system-level statistics; where distribution of ratios is complex, use Monte Carlo to estimate distributions and histograms.
